scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: El sello de Tony Wilson, presentador de televisión educado en Cambridge y admirador de los situacionistas. Peter Saville le da una identidad visual de austeridad modernista (Bauhaus, De Stijl, constructivismo); el catálogo numera cualquier cosa (FAC 8, un temporizador menstrual de Linder; FAC 99, la factura del dentista de Rob Gretton). Sin contratos, «continua negación a la ganancia» y una firme voluntad federalista frente a Londres.

podcast.title: Founder of The Haçienda (1982)
podcast.body: In 1982, he founded The Haçienda, a discotheque in Manchester that became crucial and officially launched the Manchester movement. "Poco después en 1982 fundaba la cienda que sería una discótica que sería clave en Manchester y nací oficialmente el pistoletazo de salida al movimiento Manchester."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 4. La banda tras el final

podcast.title: 2005 Interview Revelation
podcast.body: In a poignant and widely discussed 2005 interview, Tony Wilson confessed that while they knew Ian Curtis was severely unwell, they tragically underestimated the possibility of his suicide, explicitly stating that neither the band nor he were entirely surprised by the event, indicating a profound sense of remorse. "en el 2005 tuvimos una entrevista de Tony Wilson muy reveladora en la que posiblemente él nunca había sido como tan honesto y tan emocionalmente abierto hacia lo que fue la muerte de Ian Cortes. Y nos dio una visión casi que te encogí al corazón, fue como muy sonada esa entrevista a Cristiano del 2005, en la cual Tony Wilson dijo literalmente sabíamos que Ian Cortes estaba muy mal, sabíamos que no estaba bien, pero subestimamos la posibilidad de que esto pasara y daba a entender además muy clara que ni a la banda ni a él ni a nadie les sorprendió demasiado el que Ian Cortes es suicidada."

podcast.title: "24 Hour Party People" Portrayal
podcast.body: The movie "24 Hour Party People" offers a "lightly fictionalized account" of Tony Wilson's involvement with Factory Records and the vibrant Manchester music scene. "If you've ever seen the movie 24 hour party people, you have a lightly fictionalized account of what happened and I must stress that the movie is only lightly fictionalized."

xref.title: Barbados Album Budget Misuse
xref.body: While recording an album in Barbados, the band spent their entire allocated budget on drugs instead of producing the record properly. "When labelhead Tony Wilson allowed the band to record an album in Barbados, they spent their entire budget on drugs instead of making a proper record."

xref.title: Battle of the Bands and Tony Wilson
xref.body: On April 14, 1978, Joy Division competed in a Battle of the Bands at Rafters, hoping to secure a record deal. Ian Curtis, believing Tony Wilson (host of the TV show "So It Goes") needed to know about the band, approached him with an "angry, insulting letter" rather than polite conversation, which unexpectedly impressed Wilson enough to book Joy Division on his show. "Ian believed that Tony definitely needed to know about Joy Division. But instead of being all polite and respectful, Ian just slammed the guy, complete with a very angry, very insulting letter."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

xref.title: Documentaries and Biographies
xref.body: Joy Division's story is chronicled in Deborah Curtis's 1995 book "Touching From a Distance," whose title comes from the song "Transmission," and the band was also a significant part of the movie "24 Hour Party People." A feature film on Ian's life, "Control," was directed by U2 photographer Anton Corbijn and executive produced by Tony Wilson. "And one of the best rock biographies you'll ever read is a 1995 book written by Deborah Curtis called Touching From a Distance."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

xref.title: Example of Postmodern Music
xref.body: Joy Division was presented as an example of what Tony Wilson, their label boss at Factory Records, termed "postmodern music." Wilson, described as an "intellectual art snob," specifically applied this term to groups like Joy Division, intending to link the music's aesthetic to the principles of actual postmodernism in the art world. "Joy Division with level terraces apart, an example of what Tony Wilson, their label boss, termed postmodern music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Etymology: Part 1

xref.title: Factory Records Contract
xref.body: Contrary to popular myth, Happy Mondays did have a contract with Factory Records, though it might have been an unusual arrangement that allowed them considerable freedom. Tony Wilson, head of Factory Records, loved the band and let them operate with this leeway, despite much of the rest of the label, including other bands and managers, not taking to them. "We did have a contract... Tony loved us. Everyone hated us."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of Manchester Part 2

xref.title: Initial Resistance from Factory Records
xref.body: When Happy Mondays were signed to Factory Records, there was some initial skepticism and resistance from certain factions within the label, who reportedly referred to them as "football hooligans" due to their appearance. Despite this, they were allowed to perform on the label's premises to generate interest, implying Tony Wilson's support. "And I think when we went on factory, there was a lot of, by the long Colt Brigade on factories, like, you know, not them, you know."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Relationship with Factory Records Staff
xref.body: Apart from Tony Wilson, who "loved" the Happy Mondays and supported them, many other bands, managers, and staff at Factory Records "hated" them or "didn't really take tools." "Tony Loved Us, everyone hated us."

xref.title: Rob Gretton Becomes Manager
xref.body: Joy Division's performance on Tony Wilson's TV show "So It Goes" made a strong impression on Rob Gretton, who subsequently became the band's manager. "When they made it to TV, their performance impressed another guy, Rob Gretton, the person who would become Joy Division's manager."

xref.title: Tony Wilson's Vocal Suggestion
xref.body: Tony Wilson of Factory Records suggested to Ian Curtis that he try using his baritone range when singing "Love Will Tear Us Apart," in a manner similar to Frank Sinatra. Curtis adopted this suggestion, adding a "very old-school crooning" element to his vocal performance on the track. "Tony Wilson of the band's factory records made a suggestion. Ian tried using the baritone range in the same way Frank Sinatra would when you sing this song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Stories Behind Songs - 5

xref.title: Vocal Coaching Influence
xref.body: During the recording of Joy Division's "Closer" album, Ian Curtis was made to listen extensively to Frank Sinatra records by producer Martin Hannett and Tony Wilson. This unusual coaching technique was aimed at helping Ian develop a deeper, richer, and more authoritative vocal delivery, which contributed to the album's haunting sound. "Why? Because they made him listen to a lot of Frank Sinatra records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

xref.title: Voice Transformation for 'Closer'
xref.body: During the recording of the "Closer" album in March 1980, producer Martin Hannett and Factory Records head Tony Wilson coached Ian to achieve a deeper and richer vocal delivery by having him listen extensively to Frank Sinatra records, which resulted in a more haunting and authoritative sound that made his portrayals of pain and alienation highly credible. "Why? Because they made him listen to a lot of Frank Sinatra records."
